case: Kelo v. City of New London, 545 U.S. 469 (2005)
note: Legal documentary. Every numeric claim carries a source. verified:false or confidence:medium items are hedged in the script. Susette Kelo is a living private, non-convicted person (R2): symbols only, dignity, no invented quotes.

facts.claim: Kelo v. City of New London was decided 5-4, upholding the taking.
facts.detail: The Supreme Court AFFIRMED the Connecticut Supreme Court by a 5-4 vote, holding the condemnations satisfied the Fifth Amendment 'public use' requirement. The Court ruled the city COULD take the homes; it did NOT rule the taking illegal or unconstitutional.

facts.claim: Citation and date: 545 U.S. 469 (2005), No. 04-108, decided June 23, 2005.
facts.detail: On writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of Connecticut.

facts.claim: Justice John Paul Stevens wrote the majority opinion; Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer joined.
facts.detail: Five-justice majority. Kennedy also filed a separate concurrence (see F05).

facts.claim: The doctrinal move: 'public use' read broadly as 'public purpose'; economic development qualifies.
facts.detail: Stevens: 'Promoting economic development is a traditional and long accepted function of government.' The Court held that a taking executed pursuant to a carefully considered economic-development plan serves a 'public purpose' and thus satisfies the 'public use' requirement, even though the land is transferred to private developers. The majority emphasized deference to legislative judgment and did NOT hold that government may take a home for 'any reason.'

facts.claim: Kennedy's concurrence was the fifth vote and left a door open for heightened review of pretextual takings.
facts.detail: Kennedy applied rational-basis review but wrote that 'transfers intended to confer benefits on particular, favored private entities, and with only incidental or pretextual public benefits, are forbidden by the Public Use Clause,' and that some transfers may be 'so suspicious, or the procedures employed so prone to abuse, or the purported benefits are so trivial or implausible' that a presumption of invalidity could apply. He found no such evidence in this case.

facts.claim: Justice O'Connor wrote the principal dissent, joined by Rehnquist, Scalia, and Thomas.
facts.detail: Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia and Thomas joined O'Connor's dissent.

facts.claim: O'Connor verbatim (Motel 6 / Ritz-Carlton).
facts.detail: VERBATIM from the dissent: 'Nothing is to prevent the State from replacing any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton, any home with a shopping mall, or any farm with a factory.' Preceded by: 'The specter of condemnation hangs over all property.'

facts.claim: O'Connor verbatim (beneficiaries / victims).
facts.detail: VERBATIM: 'The beneficiaries are likely to be those citizens with disproportionate influence and power in the political process, including large corporations and development firms.' And: the government now 'has license to transfer property from those with fewer resources to those with more.' She also wrote the ruling effectively deletes 'the words "for public use" from the Takings Clause.'

facts.claim: Justice Thomas filed a separate originalist dissent.
facts.detail: Thomas argued the original meaning of 'public use' is use BY the public, and that reading it as 'public purpose' erased a textual limit the Founders wrote deliberately; he warned the burden of such takings falls hardest on the poor and politically powerless.

facts.claim: The Fort Trumbull redevelopment: a 90-acre plan on a New London peninsula.
facts.detail: The New London Development Corporation (NLDC), a private nonprofit reactivated by the city, drew up a plan for roughly 90 acres including a waterfront hotel/conference center, office and research space, new residences, a marina, and a riverwalk. It was projected to create jobs and increase tax revenue.

facts.claim: Pfizer's ~$300 million research facility was the economic catalyst.
facts.detail: Pfizer announced it would build a research headquarters (reported ~$300 million) adjacent to Fort Trumbull; the city built its redevelopment plan around that anchor.

facts.claim: About 115 properties were in the project area; a handful of owners refused to sell and sued.
facts.detail: The redevelopment area contained roughly 115 privately owned properties. Most owners sold; nine owners of 15 properties (including Susette Kelo) refused and challenged the condemnations. Kelo's home was on parcel 3 of the plan.

facts.claim: Susette Kelo's 'little pink house': bought 1997, on the water, restored by her.
facts.detail: Susette Kelo bought the house in 1997 for its water views and renovated it; she painted it pink. Symbolic center of the case. R2 living private person — no invented quotes, dignity framing only.

facts.claim: The Institute for Justice represented the homeowners; Scott Bullock argued the case.
facts.detail: Scott G. Bullock of the Institute for Justice presented oral argument for the plaintiffs.

facts.claim: Pfizer announced in 2009 that it would leave New London.
facts.detail: In January 2009 Pfizer announced it would close/consolidate out of its New London research facility (completed the exit around 2010-2011), eliminating more than a thousand jobs, as a major tax break was expiring. The anchor of the entire redevelopment rationale departed.

facts.claim: The condemned Fort Trumbull land sat largely vacant/undeveloped for years.
facts.detail: The planned development did not materialize; financing fell through. As of the beginning of 2010 the former Kelo parcel was a vacant lot generating no tax revenue. After Hurricane Irene (2011) the cleared area was used as a dump for storm debris. As of 2024, little had been built (a community/senior center project reported). Frame the ruling's aftermath as a failed plan, hedged to observed status.

facts.claim: The neighborhood homes were demolished; Susette Kelo's actual pink house was SAVED and relocated.
facts.detail: The Fort Trumbull homes were cleared/demolished and the site scraped. IMPORTANT NUANCE: Kelo's specific pink house was NOT destroyed — it was dismantled and relocated to 36 Franklin Street in New London (dedicated ~2008). Do NOT say her pink house was demolished; say the neighborhood was cleared and her house was moved.

facts.claim: Legislative backlash: more than 40 states enacted eminent-domain reform after Kelo.
facts.detail: Widely reported; exact count varies by source and by how 'reform' is counted. Wikipedia states 45 states had enacted some type of reform legislation as of April 2019 (citing the Institute for Justice / '50 State Report Card' tracking). Other sources cite 43, 44, or 47. SCRIPT USES the hedged, defensible framing 'more than forty states.' Exact figure held at confidence:medium.

facts.claim: Earlier precedents the majority relied on: Berman v. Parker (1954) and Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff (1984).
facts.detail: Berman (D.C. urban blight clearance, land redeveloped by private parties) and Midkiff (Hawaii land oligopoly broken up and transferred to lessees) had already read 'public use' broadly as 'public purpose.' Kelo extended this to economic development in a non-blighted area. Script keeps these as generalized description (a blighted-neighborhood case; a land-concentration case) rather than reciting docket strings.

facts.claim: New London's economic distress context: naval facility closure and 'distressed municipality' status preceded the plan.
facts.detail: New London had suffered decades of economic decline; the closure of a nearby federal Naval Undersea Warfare Center facility (mid-1990s) cost jobs, and the state had designated the city a distressed area, motivating the aggressive redevelopment push. Script uses this as generalized context ('a city that had been losing for a long time') at high confidence for the decline, medium for the specific job figure.
